archetype.name: Gunslinger (scramble-capable)
archetype.definition: An accurate, downfield-minded passer who takes his shots into tight windows and extends plays with his legs, and accepts more interceptions than most to get the big gains.

report.headline: Top-five accuracy, bottom-two turnovers: a downfield season with a costly interception tax.
report.take:
Maye arrived in year three off a 2025 that ranked among the league's best by any measure: 0.315 EPA per play, a 10.8 CPOE and 8.93 yards an attempt, all third in the league. This season looks like the same thrower with a different risk profile. His CPOE of 6.81 still ranks 4th, his bad-throw rate of 9.6% is 3rd and better than last year, and his 8.39 yards an attempt sits 1.5 above the league average. What has changed is the turnovers. Eleven interceptions rank 48th of 49, and the dossier charts all eleven as turnover-worthy, so these are not tipped-ball bad luck. His EPA per dropback has fallen to 0.16, 15th.

The value runs downfield. Throws of 10+ air yards produced 54.1 EPA, against 10.2 on everything shorter. Deep balls alone return 0.75 a play, with 8 TDs and 5 INTs, and a 17.5 CPOE says he is completing far more of them than their difficulty predicts. The short game is where drives die. Throws behind the line, mostly screens and swings, cost 29.5 EPA. Under-center dropbacks sit at -0.33 a play. Third down (-0.084) and the red zone (-0.031) are both below water. The receiving corps is narrow: DeMario Douglas and Hunter Henry are each above 0.6 EPA a target, and the backs and the second tight end barely move the needle.

The interceptions have a shape. Seven of the eleven came on throws to the left, where his EPA is negative, while the right side carries 12 TDs and 0.454 a play. That looks like a read or a coverage problem on one side rather than an arm problem. The sack picture has actually improved. His pressure-to-sack rate of 24.6% is far below the 0.405 and 0.356 of his first two seasons, even though he holds the ball longer (3.16 seconds). Scrambles more than cover that extra time: 27 of them at 0.743 EPA each, with 17 first downs. Designed runs do not work (1.11 a carry).

Schedule explains much of the timeline. Three of his first four opponents now rank among the top six defenses, and he went negative in EPA in three of those games. From Week 5 on he posted 0.337 EPA per dropback and 9.61 ANY/A, largely against bottom-tier units like the Raiders, Jets and Dolphins. The last three games are the warning. CPOE hit 10.8, but 4 picks and a 9.2% sack rate pulled efficiency below his season mark. The Packers game, with three interceptions behind a line that lost its tackle mid-game, showed both problems at once.

strengths.title: Downfield accuracy that creates points
strengths.body: He is completing difficult intermediate and deep throws well above expectation, and that is where nearly all his passing value lives. It matches his 2025, when he ranked 3rd in CPOE and YPA, so it is a skill, not a hot streak. The touchdowns on deep balls will cool somewhat, but the efficiency underneath them should hold.

strengths.title: Scrambles that pay for the hold time
strengths.body: His time to throw has crept up, but the extended plays turn into productive scrambles, 0.743 EPA apiece and 17 first downs. At the same time, his pressure-to-sack rate has fallen sharply from his first two seasons. Escaping pressure and turning it into yards is a stable trait for a mobile 24-year-old.

strengths.title: Ball placement is cleaner than ever
strengths.body: A 9.6% bad-throw rate ranks 3rd and is down from last year. Combined with his completion-over-expected, it says the misses are not accuracy misses. That puts the interception problem on decisions and coverage reads, which coaching can fix.

concerns.title: Interceptions are real, not unlucky
concerns.body: All eleven picks are charted as turnover-worthy, and his 4.0% INT rate ranks 42nd. He has always run an above-average INT rate, ranking in the 40s in both prior seasons, but this pace is a step up. Some regression toward last year is reasonable, yet this is part of who he is when he pushes the ball.

concerns.title: Left-side throws are a turnover sink
concerns.body: Seven interceptions and negative EPA come on throws to the left, while the right side is his most productive area. On over a hundred attempts that is more than a fluke. Defenses can lean coverage that way until he or the staff adjusts.

concerns.title: Short game and money downs drag
concerns.body: Screens and swings behind the line have bled EPA. Third-down and red-zone passing are below average, and under-center play-action-style dropbacks have not worked. Part of this is scheme and a weak run game (24th in rush EPA), which forces more of the offense onto his downfield throws.

trend.note: He went negative in three of four games against strong early defenses, then surged from Week 5 against softer opponents. The last three games brought big CPOE but 4 picks and more sacks, ending in a three-interception loss to Green Bay.

nextGame.headline: Worst QB defense in the league, but a patched line in front
nextGame.body:
Detroit is close to an ideal opponent for this profile. It allows the most QB fantasy points and passing yards in the league, ranks 27th in pass EPA and 28th in explosive pass rate, and is the second-strongest pass funnel, meaning offenses throw more than usual against it. The Lions' offense ranks 4th in pass EPA. Facing a New England defense that is 28th against deep passes, the 51.5 total points to a shootout. The likely game script, with New England a small underdog, should keep Maye throwing all afternoon. The catch is pressure: Detroit hits the quarterback at the 5th-highest rate. His sack rate climbed over the last three games, and that is when interceptions follow.

Availability cuts both ways. New England's left tackle Will Campbell (90% of snaps) is questionable with a knee, center Ben Brown is doubtful, and guard Van Roten remains on IR, so the interior could be a patchwork against a front that gets home. Both lead backs are compromised, with Stevenson questionable and Henderson out, which pushes even more of the offense onto Maye's arm and legs. A.J. Brown is out again, but he has played only three games and has not been central. On Detroit's side, linebacker Jack Campbell (97% of snaps) is on IR, and corner D.J. Reed (94%) and linebacker DJ Wonnum are out. That removes two every-down coverage pieces from a defense already leaking to tight ends and the middle of the field.

keyMatchups.title: Hunter Henry against a thin second level
keyMatchups.body: Detroit lets top tight ends score well above their averages, 31st in the league, and allows 0.69 EPA per TE1 target. Without Jack Campbell, the seams and middle should be open. Henry already returns over 0.6 EPA a target, and Maye's middle-of-field throws are among his most efficient.

keyMatchups.title: Detroit's rush vs a depleted line
keyMatchups.body: Detroit's hit rate ranks 5th, and New England may be without its starting left tackle and center. Maye's long time to throw invites contact. Whether he converts that pressure into scrambles or eats sacks will decide the game.

keyMatchups.title: Shootout script and pass volume
keyMatchups.body: Detroit's offense is top-five through the air, and New England's defense struggles against explosive passes. A high total and an underdog script mean volume, on top of Detroit already being a pass funnel.

nextGame.watch: Whether Campbell and Brown play. A clean pocket makes this a big yardage day, while a collapsing one brings back the sack-and-interception games.

restOfSeason.body:
The accuracy, the downfield efficiency and the scramble value are backed by two seasons and should hold. Expect him to stay a top-ten yardage and touchdown passer, especially with a run game and defense that keep pushing games toward shootouts. The interception rate should ease somewhat toward his career norm, but not all the way to last year, given how many of the throws are charted as turnover-worthy and how concentrated they are to one side. The deep-touchdown rate is the most likely number to cool.

The biggest variable is protection. With the line banged up and both lead backs hurt, he may carry more of the offense on more dangerous dropbacks. He is good enough to win that way against soft defenses, and he showed against strong ones early that he is vulnerable. I'd project roughly 255 to 295 passing yards and around two touchdowns a game, with about one interception a game remaining part of the cost.

confidence.note: Nine games split between a hard early schedule and soft later one, plus fresh line and backfield injuries.
